title: What are we?
hookLine: a humble prayer: what are we, what is our life, yet we are your people

lines: UNDER A SKY FULL OF STARS.
PROBLEMS SHRINK. SO DOES THE ONE LOOKING.
cards: Stand at the edge of the ocean at night, or under a sky far from city lights, and problems start to look smaller. So does the one looking up. It can be humbling and freeing at once.
A lot of ordinary life goes into feeling big: important, busy, needed. A few minutes into the morning, the prayer book does the opposite on purpose.
Right after the story of Abraham, it asks a question you'd expect from someone staring at the stars. What are we?

teach.b: The prayer begins: master of all worlds, we don't lay our pleas before you because of our righteousness, but because of your great mercy. Then a string of short questions: what are we?

teach.h: WHAT ARE WE? WHAT IS OUR LIFE?
teach.b: What is our life? What is our kindness, our goodness, our strength? These opening questions are old.
A version appears in the Talmud, tractate Yoma, among confessions said on Yom Kippur, and the morning prayer book borrowed them for every day. Then it piles on.

Before you, the mighty are as nothing, the well-known as if they'd never been, the wise as if they knew nothing. It even quotes Ecclesiastes: compared with the beasts, people have no advantage, for all is vanity.
If it stopped there, it would be bleak. It doesn't. The next word is but.
But we are your people, children of your covenant. Children of Abraham, whom you loved. The seed of Isaac, who was bound on the altar.
The community of Jacob. And then it turns all the way around: therefore we are obligated to thank you.
How fortunate we are, how good is our portion, how pleasant our lot. In Hebrew, ashreinu.
Small, then loved, then grateful. It doesn't ask anyone to feel important. It sets smallness and being held side by side.
A psalm asks it too: what is man, that God is mindful of him? The prayer's answer: not much, and dearly loved.

how: In many prayer books, the passage beginning 'master of all worlds' and 'what are we' follows the morning blessings and leads into ashreinu, followed by the first line of the Shema, said early in the service.

s: the prayer ends in despair about how small people are
it turns on one word, but: we are your people. then ashreinu, how fortunate we are.
the prayer says we plead because of our righteousness
not because of our righteousness, but because of your great mercy.

games.q: the prayer has just said: before you the mighty are as nothing, and all is vanity. what's the next word?
games.why: but. but we are your people, children of your covenant. the smallness turns into belonging, and then into thanks.

practice: Picture the earth from far away, one blue dot, and you somewhere on it, too small to see, and let that take the weight off. Then bring to mind one person who loves you, or loved you once, and feel how big you are to them.
Hold both pictures together; if you pray, you can say ashreinu, how fortunate we are.

wordCard.voice: Mah anu. What are we — the morning prayer's question, admitting how small people are, then turning: but we are your people, and how fortunate we are.
